Enrolled Sept. 6, 1918 5-192 BRIEF. APPLICATION OF Mrs. Eva Lewis FOR THE ENROLLMENT OF Anna Lewis IN THE INDIAN SCHOOL AT Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. POST OFFICE ADDRESS OF APPLICANT: White Swan, Wash. Date of enrollment, Sept. 6, 1918 Term of enrollment, three (3) years. NAME OF COLLECTING AGENT: Brought by her mother Position, APPLICATION FOR ENROLLMENT IN A NONRESERVATION SCHOOL. (For a child enrolled at an Agency.) For and in consideration of the United States assuming the care, education, and maintenance in the United States Indian School at Cushman Ind.Sch., Tacoma, Wash. Nina Lewis, female, I, Mrs. Eva Lewis, of White Swan P.O., State of Wash., do hereby voluntarily consent and agree to her enrollment in said school for a period of three years, and also obligate and bind myself to abide by all the rules and regulations for Indian schools. I further say that the said child was born at White Swan on Oct. 6, 1903; that the father, Mr. Lewis, was an Indian of the Yakima Tribe located at Yakima Agency; that he left the tribe about ; that the mother, Eva Lewis, is an Indian of the Yakima Tribe located at Yakima Agency, and left the tribe about ; that the said child was born and reared in the United States, and now actually resides therein; and that he has attended the following schools:

I therefore recommend that the said child be enrolled in this school. This 20 day of May, 1919 Claude A. Kinney Sept. 26-1919 S.E.C. School Physician INDORSEMENT. A child showing one-sixteenth or less Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, Indian fashion, who, if debarred from the Government schools, could not obtain an education, may be permitted in the reservation day and boarding schools, but it is preferable that it be not transferred to a nonreservation school, without special permission from the Office. Children showing one-eighth or less Indian blood, whose parents do not live on an Indian reservation, whose home is among white people where there are churches and schools, who are presumed to have adopted the white man's manners and customs, and are to all intents and purposes white people, are debarred from enrollment in the Government nonreservation and reservation schools. Superintendents, in all cases where doubt exists as to the degree of Indian blood of a child proposed for transfer, should fully satisfy themselves of the facts by affidavits from reliable persons, which affidavits must be kept on file at the school. A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both Superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and Superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. A pupil dismissed from school for cause must not be enrolled in any other school without the permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Full facts must be submitted with each request. Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., April 9, 1920 Mrs. Eva Lewis Wapato, Washington Dear Madam: Since the funds to the credit of your daughter, Nina Lewis, have been exhausted, I request that you send her a small amount in order that she may continue with her music lessons. I suggest that you send enough to cover her music lessons for this month and next month, and also a little for spending money. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. :MG Wapato, Wash. 4-5-20 Sept. C. Veel. Sir, I'm going to write you few lines asking you how is Nika Lewis. I've written to her and no answer come from her makes me feel worried about her. us poor people think of our children as much as rich people, and I've learned that nation is little to mean to the girls. It's no fair to have her call the child's mean names. She put there to teach the children what is right and wrong and not call them names so let me know what is the matter with her is she sick. I close, Yours Mrs. E.E. Lewis. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., April 7, 1920 Mrs. Eva E. Lewis Wapato, Washington Dear Madam: I am in receipt of your letter advising that you do not hear from your daughter, Nina Lewis, and requesting information in regard to her. I have to advise that I have made inquiry about Nina and I am advised that she is getting along nicely. I inquired to the Matron about her and she advises that Nina is well and is getting along nicely, only that she has a little love affair with one of the boys and as a consequence she has to discipline her somewhat. As to the Matron being a little too mean and calling the children mean names, I have to advise that this is only imagination on the part of some of the pupils. She is strict and one in that position has to be strict in order to be successful. When any of the girls misbehave, the Matron immediately corrects her and if she thinks it necessary, gives them some sort of punishment. A pupil naturally thinks that she needs never to be punished, and therefore dislikes the Matron for punishing her. Our Matron has the reputation of being one of the best in the Service and I always feel that a girl is absolutely safe when placed in her care. You no doubt love your children dearly, but children are not always considerate of their parents, and of course Nina is no exception to this rule as she apparently neglects her duty in not writing to you. You may rest assured that any discipline she gets from the Matron is for her good. However, as stated above, Nina is not a bad girl and she is getting along nicely. This school will be permanently closed at the end of this term and I trust that you will see that Nina continues her schooling next year. Assuring you of my deep interest in all the affairs of the Indians and especially the children of school age, I am Yours respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. White Swan 3-8-20 Sir, I'm very sorry to say that I didn't found what you send for. I'm sending my last letter I got, but couldn't find what you said of. I'm always out working & I'm not at home half a time so it might of been destroyed. I'm so very sorry to say it. Yours & Truly, Eva Lewis 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Feb. 21, 1920 Mrs. Eva Lewis White Swan, Washington Dear Madam: There is enclosed herewith Official Receipt No. 176172 covering the deposit of $10.00 for Nina Lewis. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Dec. 11, 1919 Mrs. Eva Lewis White Swan, Washington Dear Madam: There is enclosed herewith Official Receipt No. 176123 covering your deposit of $20.00 for Nina Lewis. Very respectfully, Superintendent :MC Inc. Nisqually Wash Nov. 6 - 19 Dept. Mr. Hammond. Dear Sir, I'm going to drop a line to you asking you again about Nina Lewis taking music lessons. Will you kindly put her on the music list. I want her to take a start. You know that I put her there just for music, so I'm sending some money for starting in music, and every month I can send money in to the office. I'll send $20.00 and if she wants little money to spend let her have some. Will you do put her in music please. I may be in town but can't go just now. Yours Truly, Mrs. Eva Lewis. CASE RECORD. Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle Mina Lewis Co. K, 44th Inf Camp Lewis Wash. Oct. 24, 1918 Dear Cousin Mina, Will drop you a few lines and let you know I am well hope you are the same. Say Mina who is your mother did she ever go back to White Swan, let me know will you? I am going to White Swan for a few days and see some of my friends. So if you want to send a word back with one please do it. Hope this few lines will make you remember you have Cousin in camp, and soon going across to France to have some fun with the Ketchumans. Write soon Nina and let me know how you are getting along. Could have did better but no time now. But will keep time if you answer. Your truly Cousin, Fred W.
